name: Lloyds Bank
scope: The privacy notice on Lloyds' personal banking website, which Lloyds Banking Group uses for its companies that provide products under the Lloyds name, including Bank of Scotland. Incidents count anywhere in the Lloyds Banking Group if they involve the Lloyds name.

A1.finding: The notice doesn't say that Lloyds gives your details to companies outside the group for their own marketing. None of the groups it says it shares data with is described as getting it for that.
A1.where: Who we share your personal information with

A2.finding: Lloyds decides what marketing you get using what you tell it and the data it collects when you use its services, and it lists payment and transaction details among that data. The reasons it gives are your consent or its legitimate interests, and you can ask it to stop. Cashback offers from shops, picked from where you have shopped, only start after you register for Offers, and you can opt out of them in the app or online banking.
A2.where: How we work out what marketing you receive; Rewards FAQs

A3.finding: The notice lists advertisers and technology providers you use, such as websites and social media, among the companies it shares data with. It says this is so you see marketing that may interest you, and so it can find new customers who are like you. It doesn't say which details it sends or whether they are scrambled first. The reasons it gives for marketing are your consent or its legitimate interests, and it says you can ask it to stop.
A3.where: Who we share your personal information with; How we work out what marketing you receive

A4.quote: not to sell your personal information
A4.finding: This is one of the promises Lloyds lists at the start of the notice.

A5.finding: The notice says Lloyds may share or sell information to organisations outside the group after it has removed personal details. Its examples are groups such as types of customers in one area who shop for clothes, and patterns of spending habits. It says this helps those organisations learn about the types of customers they have.
A5.where: Sharing information that doesn't reveal your identity

C1.finding: Not measured yet. We count trackers in a real browser, and this check is still to be done.

C2.finding: Exodus Privacy found six tracking tools in version 128.02 of the Android app: Adobe Experience Cloud, AppDynamics, Google Analytics, Google Firebase Analytics, Google Tag Manager and Qualtrics. None of them is a tool that only reports crashes, so all six count.
C2.where: Exodus report of 7 January 2024, the newest we could find

C3.finding: Not checked yet. This is checked in a real browser together with the tracker count.

C4.finding: To log in to online banking on the website you enter your user ID, your password and three characters of your memorable information. For the extra check, Lloyds texts you a passcode, or calls you and asks you to say a code shown on the screen. You can also mark a device you use often as trusted. The help pages don't mention approving the login in the app or using a card reader.

D1.finding: Lloyds says that in most cases it keeps your data for up to seven years after you stop having a product or service. It may keep it longer, for example where the law means it can't delete it. Fraud prevention agencies may keep data for up to six years.
D1.where: How long we keep your personal information

D2.finding: It lists the types of organisations it shares with, and names some of them: the credit reference agencies TransUnion, Equifax and Experian, and the card networks Visa and Mastercard.
D2.where: Who we share your personal information with

D3.finding: It explains the decisions it makes automatically, including credit scoring, fraud checks, opening accounts and pricing. It says you can object to an automated decision and ask for a person to review it.
D3.where: How we use your information to make automated decisions; Your data privacy rights

D4.finding: It says some of its systems learn from your information so that its automated decisions stay accurate and fair. It also gives training systems that learn from data as one of the ways it uses your information.
D4.where: How we use your information to make automated decisions

E1.finding: The notice says you can manage your marketing choices in online banking or the mobile app, or at a branch, and that you can tell Lloyds to stop sending you marketing at any time.

E2.finding: You can ask for a copy of your data with an online form on the Lloyds website, or print a paper form and post it. Lloyds says it answers within one month, or up to three months for complex requests.
E2.where: How to contact us; What personal information do we have about you?

sharing.why: Checking who you are and stopping fraud and money laundering

sharing.who: Police, courts, tax offices, regulators, government and the deposit guarantee scheme
sharing.why: To obey the rules that apply to the bank

sharing.who: Credit reference agencies: TransUnion, Equifax and Experian
sharing.what: Identity details, credit applications, account balances and repayment records
sharing.why: Checking who you are and what you can afford, stopping financial crime, managing accounts, collecting debts and making sure offers suit you

sharing.what: Card payment and Direct Debit details
sharing.why: To make card payments and Direct Debits work

sharing.who: Suppliers, agents, advisers, insurers and debt collectors
sharing.what: What each needs for its job. Insurance claims go on registers shared with other insurers

sharing.what: Information held across the group's brands

sharing.who: Partners and introducers, such as shops, car dealers, brokers and price comparison sites

sharing.what: Your feedback, sometimes combined with other data, and reports on general patterns
sharing.why: Understanding what customers think and improving the business

sharing.why: Showing you marketing that may interest you, and finding new customers who are like you

incidents.title: App glitch showed customers other people's transactions
incidents.summary: On 12 March 2026, a fault in an overnight software update meant some Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland app users could see other people's transactions. Lloyds told Parliament's Treasury Committee that 446,915 customers were affected, after first giving a figure of 447,936. Of these, 107,937 clicked on other people's transactions and may have seen more, such as account details, National Insurance numbers and payment references. Lloyds later said another 80,508 joint account holders may have had their transactions seen. It paid compensation for distress and inconvenience, and said it had found no customer who lost money.

notCounted.what: The Financial Conduct Authority fined Lloyds Bank, Bank of Scotland and The Mortgage Business a total of £64,046,800 for how they treated mortgage customers who had fallen behind on payments between 2011 and 2015.
notCounted.why: About how customers in mortgage arrears were treated, not privacy

notCounted.what: The Financial Conduct Authority fined four Lloyds Banking Group insurance companies, including Lloyds Bank General Insurance, a total of £90,688,400 over misleading wording in home insurance renewal letters.
notCounted.why: About misleading insurance letters, not privacy
